title: Feature Scaling II - Normalization
abstract:
The four normalization techniques from the notes — Min-Max scaling, Mean
normalization, Max-Abs scaling and Robust scaling — each with its formula, the
range it produces, the exact condition that makes it the right choice, and the
condition that makes it the wrong one. The document closes with the
standardization-versus-normalization decision rule the notes state directly:
standardization for gradient-based models, normalization for distance-based
models, neither for tree-based models.

blocks.t: The Four Normalization Techniques

blocks.cap:
One column — roughly normal around 50, with three outliers planted at
 $-40$, $210$ and $225$ — put through all five scalers. Note how Min-Max and
 Max-Abs compress the entire bulk of the data into a small sub-interval, while
 Robust leaves it spread out.

blocks.t: Min-Max Scaling
Formula

\boxed{ X_{\text{scaled}}=\frac{X_i-X_{\min}}{X_{\max}-X_{\min}} }
 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \text{range } [0,1]
From the notes: when to use it

Used when the data has fixed bounds and no outliers —
basically when you know the upper and lower bound. The canonical example
is image pixels, where the min and max are $0$ and $255$ by definition.

The transformation is a linear map that sends $X_{\min}\mapsto0$ and
$X_{\max}\mapsto1$. It preserves the shape of the distribution exactly —
like standardization, it only shifts and stretches.
One outlier destroys it

$X_{\max}$ appears in the denominator, and $X_{\max}$ is by definition the most
extreme value in the column. A single erroneous entry crushes everything else
into a narrow band near zero.
Test values escape the range

Min-Max learns $X_{\min}$ and $X_{\max}$ from the training set. A test
value larger than any training value produces a scaled value above 1. This is not
a bug — it is the correct, honest behaviour — but code that assumes $[0,1]$
(a sigmoid output layer, a fixed-range visualisation) will break. Use
clip=True only if you genuinely want to cap it, and know that you are
discarding information when you do.
Mean Normalization
Formula
\boxed{ X_{\text{scaled}}=\frac{X-X_{\text{mean}}}{X_{\max}-X_{\min}} }
From the notes

Centres the data around 0 by subtracting the mean, while dividing by the
range rather than the standard deviation. The result is approximately $[-1,1]$
and always has mean exactly 0.

It sits between Min-Max (bounded but not centred) and standardization (centred
but not bounded). It is rarely used in practice — scikit-learn has no
dedicated class for it — but it is worth knowing because it makes the
structure of all four formulas obvious: each is a choice of what to
subtract and what to divide by.
All five are the same template

$x' = (x - \text{centre})/\text{spread}$. The only decisions are which measure
of centre and which measure of spread, and each pair encodes a different
assumption about the data.
Max-Abs Scaling
Formula

\boxed{ X_{\text{scaled}}=\frac{X_i}{|X_{\max}|} }
 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \text{range } [-1,1]
From the notes: use in case of sparse data

Max-Abs divides each value by the maximum absolute value. Crucially, it
does not subtract anything, so zeros stay zeros. That single
property is the whole reason it exists.
Why sparsity matters so much

A TF-IDF matrix over a 50{,}000-word vocabulary is 99.9% zeros, and it is
stored as a sparse matrix that records only the non-zero entries. Subtracting a
mean from every cell would turn every one of those zeros into a non-zero number
— and a $10^6\times5\times10^4$ dense matrix does not fit in memory. Max-Abs
is the scaler that respects sparsity. Standardization and Min-Max both destroy
it (scikit-learn will refuse outright, raising an error on sparse input unless
you pass with_mean=False).

Typical uses: TF-IDF and bag-of-words matrices, one-hot encoded features,
count data, recommender-system interaction matrices.
Robust Scaling
Formula

\boxed{ X_{\text{scaled}}=\frac{X_i-X_{\text{median}}}{\text{IQR}} },
 \qquad \text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1
From the notes: use in case of outliers

Robust scaling replaces the mean with the median and the standard
deviation with the IQR. Both replacements are robust statistics —
they are computed from the middle of the distribution and are unaffected by how
extreme the extremes are.
Breakdown point — why this works

The breakdown point of an estimator is the fraction of the data that can
be made arbitrarily extreme before the estimate becomes arbitrarily wrong.

head: Statistic
Breakdown point
Meaning
rows: one point can move it arbitrarily far
up to a quarter of the data can be corrupted

blocks.t:
This is the precise reason Robust scaling survives the outlier that destroys
Min-Max.

Note that Robust scaling does not produce a bounded range, and it does not
remove the outliers — the outlying points remain outlying, just on a sensible
scale. Removing them is Topics 28–30.
Standardization vs Normalization

blocks.cap:
The decision table. Read the "use when" column first — the choice
 is driven by a property of the data, not by preference.

blocks.t: From the notes, stated directly

items:
Standardization is used for gradient-based models —
 Linear regression, Logistic regression, SVM.

Normalization is used for distance-based models —
 KNN, K-Means.

Neither is used for tree-based models — Decision
 Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost.

blocks.t: The reasoning behind the rule

Gradient-based models care about the condition number of the loss
surface (Topic 13). Unit variance is what improves it, so standardization is the
natural fit — and it tolerates outliers better than Min-Max.

Distance-based models care that every feature contributes comparably to
a distance. A bounded range makes each feature's maximum possible contribution
identical, which is exactly what Min-Max guarantees and standardization does not.

Tree-based models use only rank order within a feature, so every
monotone transform is a no-op.

head: Standardization
Normalization (Min-Max)
rows: Distance-based models, neural nets with bounded activations

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import sparse
from sklearn.preprocessing import (MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler, RobustScaler,
                                   StandardScaler, Normalizer)
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.r_[rng.normal(50, 12, 500), [210, 225, -40]]      # 3 planted outliers
X = x.reshape(-1, 1)

# =====================================================================
# 1. ALL FOUR, SIDE BY SIDE
# =====================================================================
results = {
    "MinMax":   MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(X).ravel(),
    "MaxAbs":   MaxAbsScaler().fit_transform(X).ravel(),
    "Robust":   RobustScaler().fit_transform(X).ravel(),
    "Standard": StandardScaler().fit_transform(X).ravel(),
    "MeanNorm": (x - x.mean()) / (x.max() - x.min()),    # no sklearn class
}
for name, v in results.items():
    bulk = v[:500]                              # the non-outlier points
    print(f"{name:9s} full [{v.min():7.3f},{v.max():7.3f}]   "
          f"bulk spans {bulk.max() - bulk.min():.3f}")
# MinMax   full [  0.000,  1.000]   bulk spans 0.310   <- crushed
# Robust   full [ -5.6  ,  10.4 ]   bulk spans 4.1     <- preserved

# =====================================================================
# 2. FROM SCRATCH -- every scaler is (x - centre) / spread
# =====================================================================
def minmax(a):    return (a - a.min()) / (a.max() - a.min())
def meannorm(a):  return (a - a.mean()) / (a.max() - a.min())
def maxabs(a):    return a / np.abs(a).max()
def robust(a):
    q1, q3 = np.percentile(a, [25, 75])
    return (a - np.median(a)) / (q3 - q1)

print("matches sklearn:",
      np.allclose(minmax(x), results["MinMax"]),
      np.allclose(maxabs(x), results["MaxAbs"]),
      np.allclose(robust(x), results["Robust"]))

# =====================================================================
# 3. WHY MAX-ABS FOR SPARSE DATA -- zeros must stay zeros
# =====================================================================
S = sparse.random(1000, 5000, density=0.001, random_state=0, format="csr")
print("stored non-zeros:", S.nnz, "of", 1000 * 5000)     # 5000 of 5,000,000

out = MaxAbsScaler().fit_transform(S)
print("still sparse:", sparse.issparse(out), "nnz:", out.nnz)   # True, 5000

try:
    StandardScaler().fit_transform(S)         # subtracting the mean would
except Exception as e:                        # densify -> 40 GB
    print("StandardScaler refuses:", type(e).__name__)
print("workaround:", StandardScaler(with_mean=False).fit_transform(S).nnz)

# =====================================================================
# 4. TEST VALUES CAN ESCAPE [0,1] -- and that is CORRECT
# =====================================================================
train = np.array([[10.], [20.], [30.]])
test  = np.array([[5.], [35.]])               # outside the training range
mm = MinMaxScaler().fit(train)
print("test scaled:", mm.transform(test).ravel())   # [-0.25  1.25]
print("clipped    :", MinMaxScaler(clip=True).fit(train).transform(test).ravel())
# clip=True gives [0. 1.] -- safe for a bounded output layer, but it
# DISCARDS the information that the test value was out of range.

# =====================================================================
# 5. WHICH SCALER FOR WHICH MODEL -- measured
# =====================================================================
n = 4000
age    = rng.uniform(20, 60, n)
salary = np.r_[rng.uniform(20_000, 150_000, n - 5), [5_000_000] * 5]  # outliers
X2 = np.c_[age, salary]
y  = (age > 40).astype(int)

for name, sc in [("none", None),
                 ("MinMax",   MinMaxScaler()),
                 ("Standard", StandardScaler()),
                 ("Robust",   RobustScaler())]:
    model = (KNeighborsClassifier(5) if sc is None
             else make_pipeline(sc, KNeighborsClassifier(5)))
    print(f"KNN + {name:9s} cv acc {cross_val_score(model, X2, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")
# none     ~0.53   MinMax ~0.62 (outliers crush it)
# Standard ~0.93   Robust ~0.97 (best -- outliers present)

# =====================================================================
# 6. DO NOT CONFUSE Normalizer WITH normalization
# =====================================================================
A = np.array([[3., 4.], [1., 2.]])
print("MinMaxScaler works down COLUMNS:\n", MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(A))
print("Normalizer works across ROWS (unit L2 norm):\n", Normalizer().fit_transform(A))
print("row norms:", np.linalg.norm(Normalizer().fit_transform(A), axis=1))  # [1. 1.]
# sklearn's Normalizer scales each SAMPLE to unit length -- used for text
# similarity and cosine distance. It is NOT the "normalization" of this topic.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE CORRECT PATTERN
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X2, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
pipe = make_pipeline(RobustScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(5)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("test accuracy:", pipe.score(X_te, y_te))
rs = pipe.named_steps["robustscaler"]
print("learned centre (median):", rs.center_.round(1))
print("learned scale  (IQR)   :", rs.scale_.round(1))
Worked Examples
Min-Max normalisation by hand
v' = \frac{v - v_{\min}}{v_{\max} - v_{\min}} = \frac{v-10}{40}

Train/test discipline. Compute $v_{\min}$ and $v_{\max}$ on the training set only. If a test value is $60$, it becomes $(60-10)/40 = 1.25$: outside $[0,1]$. That is correct behaviour, and clipping it to $1$ would hide drift.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Min-Max: $\dfrac{X_i-X_{\min}}{X_{\max}-X_{\min}}\to[0,1]$.
 Use when data has fixed known bounds and no outliers —
 image pixels $[0,255]$.

Mean Normalization:
 $\dfrac{X-X_{\text{mean}}}{X_{\max}-X_{\min}}$. Centres at 0 while
 staying bounded. Rarely used.

Max-Abs: $\dfrac{X_i}{|X_{\max}|}\to[-1,1]$. Use for
 sparse data — it subtracts nothing, so zeros stay zeros.

Robust: $\dfrac{X_i-X_{\text{median}}}{\text{IQR}}$. Use in the
 presence of outliers — median and IQR have a 25% breakdown
 point, while mean, std, min and max have 0%.

Every scaler is $(x-\text{centre})/\text{spread}$; they differ only in
 which centre and which spread.

Standardization $\to$ gradient-based models (linear, logistic,
 SVM). Normalization $\to$ distance-based models (KNN, K-Means).
 Neither $\to$ tree-based models (decision tree, random forest,
 XGBoost).

Min-Max test values can fall outside $[0,1]$ — correct behaviour, but
 it breaks code that assumes the bound.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Min-Max or Standardization — how do you decide?

Min-Max when the feature has known fixed bounds and no outliers (pixels,
percentages) and for distance-based models that want each feature's contribution
capped identically. Standardization when the data is roughly Gaussian, when
outliers exist, and for gradient-based models where unit variance improves the
condition number.
Q. Why is Max-Abs the only scaler safe for sparse matrices?

Because it does not subtract a centre. Every other scaler subtracts a mean,
median or minimum, which turns the stored zeros into non-zeros, densifies the
matrix and blows up memory.
Q. A test value scales to 1.4 with Min-Max. Bug or not?

Not a bug. The scaler learned its min and max from training data, and this test
value exceeds the training maximum. It is honest behaviour. It only matters if
downstream code assumes $[0,1]$ — then use clip=True and accept the
information loss.
Q. Why is Robust scaling robust?

Because the median and IQR have a breakdown point of 25% — up to a quarter of
the data can be arbitrarily corrupted before they move meaningfully. The mean,
standard deviation, minimum and maximum all have a breakdown point of 0%: one
bad value moves them arbitrarily far.
Q. Should you scale one-hot encoded columns?

Generally not. They are already in $[0,1]$ and standardising them distorts the
interpretation of the coefficients and destroys sparsity. If the pipeline forces
it, Max-Abs leaves them unchanged.
Q. Does Min-Max change the distribution's shape?

No. Like standardization it is a linear map — shift and stretch. Skewness is
unchanged. Only non-linear transforms (Topics 18–19) reshape a distribution.
